questions.q: How does Greene say you should choose the skill you want to master?
a: Trust the gut feeling that tells you what fits you
Pick whichever field currently pays the most
Follow the choice your parents recommend
Choose the subject you were best at in school
questions.why: Lesson 1 urges readers to listen to the inner voice that says a particular discipline is made for them.

questions.q: Why does Greene recommend taking a low-paying apprenticeship?
a: Learning and mentorship pay off far more than a bigger salary now
Low-paying jobs are less demanding and leave time for hobbies
Apprenticeships guarantee a job at the same company forever
Salary matters more than skill, so you should switch later
questions.why: Lesson 2 says learning has a much higher return than earning a little more early on.

questions.q: What did Benjamin Franklin do instead of joining his father’s candle business?
a: He took a printing job to master the art of words
He became a sailor to see the wider world
He opened his own shop selling imported goods
He studied law at a university abroad
questions.why: Lesson 2 uses Franklin’s printing apprenticeship as an example of choosing learning over an easier family business.

questions.q: What should you do once your apprenticeship ends?
a: Question what you learned and develop your own style
Follow your mentor’s methods exactly from then on
Stop studying because your training is complete
Teach others before attempting original work
questions.why: Lesson 3 says you must keep an open mind, challenge the rules you were taught and let your own style flourish.

questions.q: What common belief about mastery does the book set out to disprove?
a: That masters are simply born with exceptional talent
That practice matters more than natural ability
That mentors are essential to becoming great
That mastery takes many years of dedicated work
questions.why: The overview says the book debunks the myth of talent and presents steps anyone can follow toward mastery.
